name: Childersburg Industrial Park
heading: 3. Childersburg Industrial Park — 500 MW proposed
brief: In Talladega County, a proposed $6 billion, 500 MW hyperscale data center would reuse part of the former Alabama Army Ammunition Plant. The mayor described roughly 486 acres in the early agreement, a glycol-based cooling system, and approximately 220 permanent jobs if developed. Inside Climate News documented those figures from the January 2026 city meeting. The site is environmentally sensitive because of its munitions-production history; EPA documents describe the legacy cleanup obligations. The project remains proposed . Childersburg’s council took further land-redevelopment action in October, but the mayor said on October 20 that a final decision had not been made. The publicly discussed 500 MW is a proposed electrical requirement, not delivered power. Read the October update .
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alabama (2026): Full Power, Cost and Development Report

name: Project Marvel, Bessemer
heading: 2. Project Marvel, Bessemer — up to 1,200 MW proposed
brief: Project Marvel near Bessemer is a proposed multi-building campus backed by TPA Group’s Logistic Land Investment and associated with QTS Data Centers. The expanded layout calls for 18 large data-center buildings , substations, retention infrastructure and up to 1.2 GW at full development. The reported capital estimate is approximately $14 billion , but that is not money already spent. A 900-plus-acre rezoning proposal would expand the overall campus toward 1,600 acres. DCD’s filing review and WBRC’s local reporting provide the planning context. Local approval and construction records have evolved during 2026. The 1.2 GW represents a proposed ultimate buildout, and actual utility energization would require substantial new substation and transmission capacity. Neighbors have raised questions about land use, noise, power demand and environmental review. The project’s status should not be confused with completion or commissioning.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alabama (2026): Full Power, Cost and Development Report

name: Project Red Clay, Lowndes County
heading: 1. Project Red Clay, Lowndes County — up to 1,500 MW requested
brief: Cloverleaf Infrastructure’s Project Red Clay is the largest publicly tracked Alabama proposal by reported power request: 1,500 MW from Alabama Power. The development near Burkville/Hayneville includes plans for four large data buildings and supporting structures. Sources differ on land footprint—early public plans cited roughly 800 acres, while a July stormwater permit identified about 1,044 acres. These numbers describe different planning documents and dates. See the dated project evidence and Lowndes County’s official project materials . On October 13, the Lowndes County Commission approved a tax and development agreement in a 3–2 vote, advancing—but not completing—the proposal. WSFA reported the vote . The developer’s official project website promises closed-loop cooling, self-funded electrical infrastructure, more than 1,000 construction jobs and local community funding. Opponents have questioned transparency, water availability, power-rate protections and environmental effects. A reported 1.5 GW power request does not establish that the campus has 1.5 GW of contracted IT load or
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alabama (2026): Full Power, Cost and Development Report

name: STaX Franklin Bluffs Bitcoin Mining Pilot
heading: 3. STaX Franklin Bluffs Bitcoin Mining Pilot — 50 MW proposed
brief: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources recorded a May 2025 permit application from STaX Capital Partners for up to 30 acres of pad space roughly 35 miles south of Deadhorse. STaX described multiple 10 MW mobile gas-turbine generators intended to supply 50 MW of modular Bitcoin mining pods in a temporary first-phase proof of concept. This is a mining proposal , not a completed hyperscale AI data center. The public notice listed an intended July 2025–July 2029 permit term; that schedule does not establish the project received its permit or began operating. On-site power generation could reduce dependence on the Railbelt grid, but gas supply, emissions permits, fiber, land access and Arctic maintenance would still matter. For context on the sector’s wider infrastructure choices, see our Bitcoin-mining heat reuse ranking .
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alaska (2026): Power, Permits and What Is Actually Proposed

name: DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea Computing Hub
heading: 2. DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea Computing Hub — 100 MW proposed generation
brief: Near Nikiski, DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV has requested a federal preliminary study permit for an underwater compute concept. The September 4 Federal Register notice describes about 330–350 tidal turbines , 66 subsea-compute pods and approximately 3.5 miles of hybrid power/fiber cable to shore. Its estimated 100 MW is potential generation, chiefly intended for the underwater data center—not verified compute load. A preliminary permit, even if later granted, would confer study priority rather than authorize construction. The proposal faces questions about underwater thermal effects, fisheries, endangered beluga habitat and vessel activity. The public FERC docket timeline records interventions from local governments and other parties. Comments and competing filings are due November 2, 2026, at 5 p.m. Eastern . That is a live regulatory deadline, not an opening date. The Cook Inlet concept illustrates an engineering distinction that often disappears from project headlines: cooling water, turbine output and server demand form separate systems. A 100 MW tidal-array claim does not mean 100 MW
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alaska (2026): Power, Permits and What Is Actually Proposed

name: STAK Energy North Slope Campus
heading: 1. STAK Energy North Slope Campus — 1–3 GW proposed on-site generation
brief: STAK Energy’s proposal is the largest named Alaska computing campus with a disclosed power-design range. The state’s May 12, 2026, preliminary lease notice concerns 715.4 acres about 26 miles south of Deadhorse. Plans involve modular high-performance computing, an on-site gas-fired power plant, associated utilities and 1–3 GW of planned generation at potential full scale. The crucial qualifier is that 3,000 MW is the upper end of the proposed generation design , not an approved 3 GW IT connection or capacity already built. The preliminary state-land decision is not a final lease, and a new gas pipeline would require a separate process. Alaska Public Media’s May reporting described a proposed $500 million development; other developer-scale figures are higher. Those values should not be combined into a single verified construction budget. Remote gas availability and cold ambient conditions are potential advantages, but they are not proof of financial viability. The campus would still need generation and gas infrastructure, fiber connectivity, air-quality compliance, permafrost-sensitiv
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Alaska (2026): Power, Permits and What Is Actually Proposed

name: Beale Luckett Road, Marana
heading: 3. Beale Luckett Road, Marana — up to 1,500 MW planned
brief: Beale Infrastructure’s Luckett Road campus spans approximately 600 acres west of Interstate 10 in Marana. The coordinated development comprises two adjacent parcels of roughly 300 acres each. According to the Town of Marana’s official project FAQ , each parcel has an estimated 550–750 MW electrical demand, yielding a 1,100–1,500 MW combined planning range rather than 1.5 GW of installed servers. Tucson Electric Power and Trico Electric Cooperative would serve different parts of the project, and regulated utility agreements are still required. The Marana Town Council approved rezoning on January 6, 2026 , not final construction or utility energization. The town describes air-cooled equipment and prohibits use of municipal potable water for cooling. Beale forecasts construction beginning around 2027, with initial occupancy potentially in late 2028 or early 2029. Updated local noise and decommissioning requirements add another layer of oversight. These remain developer expectations, not evidence of construction completion. The campus’s full-buildout upper figure ties Hassayampa Ranch’s
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Arizona (2026): Full Power and Development Report

name: Hassayampa Ranch, West Valley
heading: 2. Hassayampa Ranch, West Valley — up to 1,500 MW proposed
brief: Arizona Land Consulting, led by Anita Verma-Lallian, and investors including Chamath Palihapitiya acquired roughly 2,100 acres for $51 million in 2025 near Tonopah and Buckeye. The developer has discussed a potential 1.5 GW power opportunity and as much as $25 billion in eventual investment if future data-center tenants build out the property. The $25 billion is a potential long-range development value, not verified spending. The developer’s own publication of the Bloomberg report says a utility agreement remains a next step. Maricopa County approved an industrial rezoning on April 8, 2026 after negotiations over setbacks and buffers. County hearing documents confirm the zoning request; local reporting describes the revised community terms. The approved zoning does not mean an end user has leased the entire campus or that 1.5 GW is available today. A recent October 13 follow-up from the reporter who visited the site still described the land as undeveloped. A separate 1 GW number appears in some zoning trackers; this ranking uses the upper developer-reported 1.5 GW potential and label

name: Tract Buckeye Technology Park
heading: 1. Tract Buckeye Technology Park — up to 1,800 MW planned
brief: Tract’s official Buckeye project page lists 2,019 acres and 1,800 MW of potential capacity for a master-planned technology park west of Phoenix. The developer’s August 2024 acquisition release originally described 2,069 acres, up to 20 million square feet and as many as 40 future data-center buildings, supported by long-term utility planning. The acreage figures reflect differing dated descriptions of the property; neither is a completed-building count. The local video above shows the project as reported at its announcement; it is not evidence that the full 1.8 GW campus has since been built. Tract markets individual parcels to data-center operators and continues power-infrastructure planning. The ultimate electrical requirement could change as tenants, substations and phases are finalized. Read the original station report .
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Arizona (2026): Full Power and Development Report

name: Google West Memphis
heading: 3. Google West Memphis — 270 MW indicative demand estimate; actual campus load undisclosed
brief: Google announced $4 billion of Arkansas investment through 2027 in October 2025, anchored by its first state data center on more than 1,000 acres in West Memphis. Construction is underway. The Arkansas government’s February 2026 water-demand planning presentation estimated approximately 270 MW initial baseload for West Memphis using an assumed watts-per-square-foot ratio. This is a planning estimate, not Google’s announced critical IT load . The same presentation does not specify a verified full-buildout MW figure. A major new development arrived on October 19, 2026 : Entergy Arkansas announced an expanded service agreement for Google’s campus, subject to regulatory review. The utility described two new 230 kV transmission lines, expansion of the Galet substation, 440 MW of solar generation and additional battery storage. It projects at least $500 million in incremental customer savings from 2028 over twenty years, on top of its earlier $1.6 billion pledge; those are utility projections, not realized bill reductions. name: Serverfarm Clarksville
heading: 2. Serverfarm Clarksville — 432 MW stated campus design
brief: Serverfarm’s Clarksville ARK campus in Johnson County is among Arkansas’s most advanced projects. Its first 300,000-square-foot building was topped out in October. Data Center Dynamics reported October 12 that the first building is planned for 108 MW , with four buildings totaling 432 MW at full development. An October Arkansas Business investigation describes roughly 430 MW for the first four buildings and a $6.6 billion development supported by up to 40 gas turbines. Later phases could change the ultimate campus footprint; do not add speculative capacity beyond the four-building figure. Serverfarm says its closed-loop cooling recirculates water, reducing consumption relative to conventional evaporative cooling. The company also plans substantial behind-the-meter natural-gas generation , limiting dependence on the municipal grid while introducing air-emissions and pipeline questions. Its first phase targets early 2028. Community discussion has focused on local utility rates, water demand, noise and the terms of the development agreement. Construction progress does not mean the full

name: AVAIO Digital Leo, Pulaski County
heading: 1. AVAIO Digital Leo, Pulaski County — 1,070 MW total baseload design
brief: AVAIO Digital’s current official campus specifications advertise 1,070 MW total baseload power , comprising 570 MW of planned grid supply and 500 MW of behind-the-meter power . The company first announced the project in January with an initial 150 MW Entergy contract and a potential 1 GW expansion. These figures describe supply architecture and buildout plans, not 1,070 MW of operating IT equipment. The current project page describes a 296-acre developed site, while the original announcement discussed a broader 760-acre campus—different site-scope descriptions that should not be conflated. The Arkansas Economic Development Commission’s January announcement described an initial $6 billion investment and potential full development exceeding $21 billion , along with more than 500 permanent jobs. AVAIO’s current site page says groundbreaking has occurred and contracted initial power is targeted online in 2027. Regulatory requirements, construction phasing and tenant commitments will determine how much capacity is ultimately used.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Arkansas (2026): Full Power, Cost and Construction Report

name: Google Disk Drive, North San José
heading: 3. Google Disk Drive, North San José — 250 MW disputed computing and research facility
brief: Google has applied to develop up to three research-and-development buildings totaling about 482,790 square feet at 5079–5087 Disk Drive and nearby parcels. The City of San José’s official project notice lists an onsite switching station, substation and associated equipment with 250 MW capacity . Separately, CPUC draft Resolution E-5455 describes a proposed PG&E agreement for a 250 MW Google load at 5079 Disk Drive, with a projected December 2028 service date. The classification is contested. San José Spotlight interviewed engineers who say the proposed cooling and electrical design resembles a data center. Google counters that the development is a research laboratory supporting internal chip engineering and lacks standard backup generation for customer-facing data centers. We include it as a large computing-related power proposal, not a confirmed commercial data center . The CPUC’s draft agreement was still awaiting a decision scheduled for October 29, according to the latest reporting.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in California (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Development Report

name: Golden Valley Technology Hub, Kern County
heading: 2. Golden Valley Technology Hub, Kern County — 275 MW planned
brief: Beacon Data Centers and California Resources Corporation propose a 275 MW AI-oriented campus at the Elk Hills Oil Field outside Taft. The project would cover about 100 acres , with approximately 400,000 square feet of computing space, an electrical substation and office facilities. The June developer announcement reported by Data Center Dynamics establishes the proposed 275 MW figure; it is not energized capacity. The Golden Valley plan differs from conventional grid-dependent campuses: it would use power from CRC’s existing Elk Hills generating plant, with grid access as backup, and recirculating liquid cooling. The developer’s FAQ states that construction timing is not yet determined and environmental review, permitting and commercial agreements remain outstanding. KERO’s on-location reporting features CRC executive Chris Gould and local residents discussing economic opportunity and environmental questions. The proposed project has not been commissioned.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in California (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Development Report

name: Prologis STEM Park, San José
heading: 1. Prologis STEM Park, San José — 396 MW planned data centers
brief: Prologis STEM Park is the largest documented California proposal in this ranking. The developer’s conceptual plan for approximately 159 acres of city-owned land near Zanker Road and the San José–Santa Clara Regional Wastewater Facility includes four data-center buildings at 99 MW each , or 396 MW total . A separate advanced-manufacturing component is estimated at 100 MW and is not included in the 396 MW data-center ranking. The City of San José’s official project memorandum lists the building-by-building electrical and floor-area figures. San José selected Prologis as its preferred developer in November 2025, but that selection is not final approval to build or operate the campus. The project also proposes roughly 785,000 square feet of advanced manufacturing, bringing the combined development beyond 2.4 million square feet. Campus project specifications describe an initial utility-power pathway of 250 MW, dependent on future arrangements and infrastructure. Environmental review, land agreements and phased utility service are still essential. October local reporting documents Prologi

name: Westbridge Fontus
heading: 3. Westbridge Fontus — 380+ MW proposed data-center capacity
brief: Westbridge Renewable Energy announced Fontus in July 2025 as a 380+ MW Colorado campus , near major population centers and a carrier-neutral fiber hub. Westbridge says it has secured the land, completed environmental-feasibility assessments and identified available fiber. The company is still pursuing electrical grid and natural-gas interconnections . Its current Fontus project page does not establish a construction start date or fully energized server capacity. Fontus is closer to an early-stage, power-ready site than a commissioned hyperscale facility. Its exact Colorado address is not publicly established in the documents reviewed, and neither an anchor tenant nor completed utility interconnection is confirmed. An October 2025 issuer-sponsored research report also describes at least 380 MW of expected demand and outlines the need for utility and gas connections. Any final buildout could differ materially from that preliminary estimate.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Colorado (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Community Report

name: Vantage Trident
heading: 2. Vantage Trident — approximately 500 MW total demand, 334 MW IT load
brief: Vantage Data Centers is advancing a contested two-building campus near East 48th Avenue and E-470 in Aurora , next to the Green Valley Ranch area. In a written statement to Capital & Main , Vantage vice president Mark Freeman described 334 MW of computing capacity and approximately 500 MW total electrical demand when computing plus cooling and other facility overhead are counted. The proposal encompasses about 143 acres and more than 860,000 square feet in two two-story buildings; it is not operating at those loads. The video provides direct local reporting about the Aurora regulatory fight, not footage proving Trident is built. The project’s location has drawn objections over diesel-generator emissions, sound, proximity to homes, water use and the lack of an automatic public hearing for certain industrial-zoned proposals. Colorado Public Radio reported October 27 that Aurora council again failed to advance a proposed moratorium after a 6–5 procedural vote that required seven votes to reconsider. Existing applications, including Trident, were not subject to the proposed pause. Meanwh

name: Cielo Hudson
heading: 1. Cielo Hudson — 750 MW proposed power capacity
brief: The largest reported Colorado proposal is Cielo Digital Infrastructure’s Hudson campus in Weld County. Rocky Mountain PBS reported in July that the project could cover approximately 500 acres and require 750 MW of power capacity . An Axios September analysis independently listed Hudson as Colorado’s largest planned data-center development. It is still proposed , and a firm construction commencement, fully signed IT-load commitment and energization date are not established in the reviewed sources. Hudson’s scale helped fuel debate in nearby Lochbuie, where the town board voted 6–1 for a five-year moratorium on new or expanded local data-center applications. That moratorium applies inside Lochbuie, not automatically to Hudson ; it should not be misreported as a cancellation of Cielo’s project. Data-center registries including SignalData list Hudson at 750 MW, while the underlying public descriptions do not consistently identify the figure as critical server load rather than overall campus power. A planning figure is not evidence of an energized substation or operational facility.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Colorado (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Community Report

name: New Britain Energy & Innovation Park
heading: 3. New Britain Energy & Innovation Park — 44 MW proposed computing phase
brief: At 480 Myrtle Street , the former Stanley Black & Decker complex has already received a substantial piece of energy infrastructure: a 19.98 MW fuel-cell installation . But the associated 44 MW high-performance-computing center was described separately as a future phase in EIP Investment’s Connecticut Siting Council petition . It would reuse older industrial buildings and be followed by additional generation, computing and technology development. The originally discussed $1 billion figure covered the broader redevelopment vision, not an already funded data center. O&G Industries confirms completion of the initial 19.8 MW fuel-cell plant and describes the computing center as a later-stage concept. The September 2026 project registry still classifies the 44 MW computing phase as proposed, with no confirmed tenant or data-center construction . The 2018 origin makes this the least current proposal in the Top 3; the first phase’s completion must not be mistaken for completion of the separate data center.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Connecticut (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Development Report

name: O&G Industries Beacon Falls
heading: 2. O&G Industries Beacon Falls — 100 MW marketed capacity
brief: A former quarry near Lopus Road and Route 8 is being offered for a data center that 2026 commercial marketing materials describe as 100 MW and approximately 294,000 square feet . The concept includes on-site natural-gas fuel cells, but neither a named hyperscale tenant nor a firm 100 MW IT-power contract is established. The property was previously the subject of a 32 MW municipal agreement in 2022. That agreement expired in 2023 without a buyer. The status is more tentative than the new brochure might suggest. In an October 25 CT Mirror investigation , First Selectman Gerry Smith said there was no active municipal proposal . He acknowledged a summer inquiry from O&G, but said no specifics followed. Neighbors have requested clearer zoning rules and scrutiny of emissions, water, noise and community benefits. This entry ranks a marketed opportunity , not an approved or funded 100 MW construction project.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Connecticut (2026): Full Power, Permitting and Development Report

name: Global Common Cromwell
heading: 1. Global Common Cromwell — more than 300 MW potential IT power
brief: Global Common is marketing a 159-acre campus around Geer Street in Cromwell with approximately 40 MW of initial IT power and a possible full buildout exceeding 300 MW IT . Unlike the other entries, the developer explicitly identifies the power figure as computing load. The plan would use natural-gas fuel cells supplied through interstate pipeline infrastructure. Global Common says it has a gas supply agreement with Emera Energy and is seeking long-term firm transportation service from Enbridge. Global Common estimates initial computing power could be delivered 18–21 months after equipment deposits , with 300+ MW available 26–32 months after deposits or over multiple phases. Those timelines are developer projections, not an announced commissioning date. WFSB’s October 24 reporting confirms no formal site-plan application had been filed . The company expects to seek site-plan approval in early 2027, while neighbors near schools and homes question potential noise, air emissions, zoning procedures and land-use compatibility. name: Data Canopy Newark
heading: 3. Data Canopy Newark — 6 MW Building Power (Operating)
brief: At 350 Pencader Drive in Newark , Data Canopy’s current operator specification gives the facility 6 MW of building power , supported by three utility feeds. The listing describes 16,085 square feet of white space , 2N and N+1 uninterruptible-power-system arrangements, Generac generators and more than 60 hours of on-site fuel supply. This is a standing enterprise colocation and managed-hosting site, not a newly announced 6 MW buildout. That distinction matters. A nameplate electrical figure may include auxiliary infrastructure, cooling and resilience headroom; it does not state the load presently drawn by customer servers. The facility’s operating history also predates the present wave of large AI campus proposals. In scale and power topology, Newark represents the kind of established, comparatively compact colocation asset that a list focused only on proposed megaprojects would miss.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Documented Data Center Projects in Delaware (2026): Power, Permits and What Is Actually Operating

name: DāSTOR New Castle
heading: 2. DāSTOR New Castle — 8 MW Power (Operating)
brief: At 3 Boulden Circle in New Castle , DāSTOR explicitly specifies 8 MW of power for a 61,000-square-foot building, along with generator-backed power, 2N+1 UPS, 2N networking and N+1 cooling. The company announced its acquisition in April 2024 , citing more than 30,000 square feet of raised floor space. The 61,000-square-foot number is total building footprint, not white-space floor area. The 8 MW figure is therefore independently traceable to the present operator rather than a broker’s projected campus demand. DāSTOR also lists a separate 4 MW facility at 1201 North Market Street in Wilmington; that site does not outrank the 6 MW Newark operation and is not combined with its New Castle sister facility. A proposed 800 MW or 1 GW utility load cannot be treated as equivalent to these operating specifications without a clear project-status label.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Documented Data Center Projects in Delaware (2026): Power, Permits and What Is Actually Operating

name: Middletown Technology Center
heading: 1. Middletown Technology Center — 50 MW Historical Projected Demand (Not Verified Built)
brief: The largest defensible non-cancelled historical development figure in this narrow documented set belongs to the Middletown Technology Center , proposed by Cirrus Delaware on land within the Middletown Auto Park. The original 2016 air-permit application specifies 50 MW projected demand at completion , with power-generation equipment capable of 62.5 MW . The difference was a 12.5 MW redundant generation allowance —not an additional 12.5 MW of server demand. The filing described approximately 60 acres of land and a natural-gas generation configuration. The reporting chronology requires care. An earlier 2015-era development account used 40 MW of data-center capacity and 52.5 MW of on-site generation for a 228,000-square-foot plan. The later application used the 50/62.5 MW design scenario. Those are successive descriptions of one scheme, not two separate facilities. In 2016, residents challenged the accompanying gas-fired plant over emissions and local impacts, as documented by Delmarva Public Media .
